text: The p-value is the most reported and most misunderstood number in statistics. Studies have found that many working researchers, and plenty of textbooks, describe it incorrectly. As a data scientist you'll be handed p-values constantly and asked to say what they mean, so this lesson is about being precise.

The exact definition: the p-value is the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one you observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Every word matters — it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data. The permutation test from last lesson gave 0.0343; a classical t-test on the same data gives nearly the same answer, 0.0346.

A p-value of 0.035 does not mean there's a 3.5 percent chance the null is true — the p-value already assumes the null is true, so it can't also be the probability of it. It doesn't mean there's a 96.5 percent chance the effect is real either, same error flipped. And it doesn't mean the effect is large or important — the p-value mixes effect size and sample size, so it says nothing about magnitude on its own.

Before running the test, choose a significance level, alpha, most often 0.05. If p falls below alpha, you call the result statistically significant and reject the null. That 0.05 threshold is a convention, not a law of nature — some fields use 0.01 or stricter, depending on how costly a false alarm is. Always report the actual p-value, not just whether it beat 0.05.

Run an A-A test — both groups come from the exact same population, so the null is actually true. Repeating it 5,000 times and collecting p-values: about 4.88 percent fall below 0.05, and the whole distribution is spread almost perfectly evenly between 0 and 1.

That's exactly what alpha equals 0.05 promises — a 5 percent false-alarm rate when nothing is actually going on. It also shows that one significant result out of many attempts is not surprising at all — a problem Lesson 26, multiple comparisons, tackles head-on.

Now the opposite scenario: a real but tiny difference — 30 cents on a 55 dollar order — with 200,000 customers per group. The p-value comes out astronomically small, 1.8 times 10 to the negative 15, yet the actual difference is only about 0.025 standard deviations, well under a dollar.

With enough data, any tiny difference becomes significant. Always pair a p-value with an effect size and a confidence interval, and ask whether the size of the effect actually matters to the business — not just whether it cleared a threshold.

To recap: a p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It's not the probability the null is true, and not a measure of effect size. Alpha, often 0.05, is a decision threshold chosen in advance. When the null is true, p-values are spread evenly, so 5 percent land under 0.05 by pure luck.
